title: Throne Inheritance
statement:
A royal family starts with just the king; people are born and die over time. Build a class `ThroneInheritance` that tracks the family and reports the line of succession.

The line of succession is built from the full family tree, dead people included. It starts with the king. To find who comes after the person `x` most recently added, look at `x`'s children from oldest to youngest (the order of their births) and take the first one not yet in the line. If every child of `x` is already in the line (or `x` has none), repeat that search from `x`'s parent instead, and so on upward; once the king himself has no child left to add, the line is complete. This process always yields one well-defined order.

- `ThroneInheritance(kingName)` starts the family with the king named `kingName`.
- `birth(parentName, childName)` records that `parentName` had a new child `childName`, younger than all of `parentName`'s earlier children.
- `death(name)` marks `name` as dead. This does not change the family tree or how the line is built.
- `getInheritanceOrder()` returns the line of succession as a list of names, leaving out everyone who has died.
constraints: kingName, parentName, childName and name consist of lowercase English letters only
kingName and all childName values are distinct
Every name passed to death was given earlier to the constructor or as a childName to birth
parentName is alive whenever birth(parentName, childName) is called
At most 10^5 calls are made to birth and death in total
At most 10 calls are made to getInheritanceOrder
notes:
## Intuition

The successor rule looks complicated, but it is exactly how a **pre-order traversal** of the family tree visits people: a person, then their oldest child's whole branch, then the next child's branch, and so on. So if each person keeps their children in birth order, the line of succession is just a depth-first walk from the king. Deaths never change the tree, so they only need a set of names to skip when printing. Simulating the rule literally (as the brute force does) rescans children and climbs back up the tree, which is far slower.

## Approach

1. Store `children`, a map from each name to the list of their children in birth order, and `dead`, a set of names.
2. `birth` appends the child to its parent's list and gives the child an empty list.
3. `death` just adds the name to `dead`.
4. `getInheritanceOrder` runs an iterative pre-order DFS: pop `person` from `stack`, add them to `order` unless they are dead, then push their `kids` from youngest to oldest so the oldest is popped next.

## Example 1, step by step

After the six births, `king` has `[andy, bob, catherine]`, `andy` has `[matthew]` and `bob` has `[alex, asha]`. The walk pops `king`, then `andy`, then `matthew` (andy's branch ends), then `bob`, `alex`, `asha`, and finally `catherine`. After `death("bob")`, the same walk runs but `bob` is skipped while his children stay: `["king", "andy", "matthew", "alex", "asha", "catherine"]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1) for `birth` and `death`; O(n) for `getInheritanceOrder`, where n is everyone ever born.
- Space: O(n) for the map, the set, and the stack during a walk.

## Pitfalls

- Do not delete dead people from the tree: their descendants still inherit in the same place.
- Push children in reverse so the oldest comes off the stack first; pushing them in order reverses every family.
- A recursive DFS can be 10^5 levels deep when each child is born to the previous one, which may overflow the call stack; an explicit stack avoids that.
- Use a `Map` rather than a plain object: names such as `constructor` clash with built-in object keys.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `king` | the root of the family tree |
| `children` | each name mapped to their children, oldest first |
| `dead` | names of people who have died |
| `order` | the line of succession being built |
| `stack` | people still to visit in the DFS |
| `person` | the person just taken from the stack |
| `kids` | `person`'s children |

narration.3: Remember the king: every line of succession starts from him.
narration.4: Each person maps to their children in birth order; the king starts with none.
narration.5: Dead people are only marked, never removed from the tree.
narration.9: Append the newborn to the end of the parent's list, so it is the youngest child.
narration.10: Give the newborn an empty list of children of their own.
narration.14: Death changes nothing in the tree; just remember the name.
narration.18: The line of succession being built.
narration.19: The depth-first walk starts at the king.
narration.20: Keep walking while someone is still waiting to be visited.
narration.21: Take the next person in pre-order.
narration.22: Living people go into the line; dead ones are skipped.
narration.23: Add this living person to the line.
narration.25: Look up this person's children, oldest first.
narration.26: Go through them from youngest to oldest...
narration.27: ...so the oldest child ends up on top of the stack and is visited next.
narration.30: Every branch was walked in order; return the line.
